tip_title: Before the Storm Hits, Your Yard Might Be Your Biggest Insurance Problem
topic: Hurricane Preparedness - Property Protection Before a Storm
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Before the Storm Hits, Your Yard Might Be Your Biggest Insurance Problem**

We're in peak Atlantic hurricane season right now, and here's something most homeowners don't think about until it's too late: anything unsecured in your yard becomes a projectile in hurricane-force winds. That patio furniture, that loose tree branch hanging over your roof, the decorative stuff sitting along your fence line — all of it. Standard homeowners policies cover sudden wind damage, but a claim gets complicated fast when the damage could have been prevented with basic prep. FEMA recommends trimming or removing trees that could fall onto your house and clearing yard debris before a storm is ever named.

Take thirty minutes this weekend to walk your yard with fresh eyes. It's the kind of thing that can make a real difference in whether you're filing a claim or just cleaning up.

Not sure how your policy handles wind damage or what your hurricane deductible looks like? Your Peachy agent can pull up your declarations page and walk through it with you.

📖 [Learn more from FEMA](https://www.fema.gov/blog/six-ways-prepare-your-home-hurricane)
summary: Covers pre-storm property preparation as an insurance risk-reduction step, specifically securing yard items and trimming trees that could cause wind damage — framed as a mid-peak-season action item distinct from prior tips on hurricane deductibles and declaration page checks.
scoring_notes: August is statistically peak Atlantic hurricane season. Both East Cobb audiences are high-homeowner (78%), so this lands well for both. Prior hurricane tips covered the declaration page review (June 22), the wind/hurricane percentage-deductible mechanic (July 24), and a NFIP vs. private flood comparison (July 20). This tip takes a completely different angle — physical property prep as a claims-prevention and coverage-context action item — so no meaningful overlap. High actionability because the reader can literally go outside this weekend.
